transcript:
[00:00] Samira Khan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:04] Maya Patel: Maya here. Owen?
[00:06] Owen Lee: Owen on. Priya in the room.
[00:09] Priya Rao: Hi.
[00:11] Samira Khan: Great. Ethan from Redwood is also with me.
[00:14] Ethan Blake: hey all, Ethan (SE) joining.
[00:20] Liam Torres: Liam here. Quick note — rough agenda: test results, integration questions, security follow-ups, next steps.
[02:05] Samira Khan: Cool so Owen you ran the SDK integration tests last week, curious what you hit?
[02:20] Owen Lee: Yeah so we wired the Redwood SDK into our microservice. We used the node sdk example you sent but tweaked it for our request/response flow — function calling to invoke enrichment tools. Latency was mostly okay, median 140ms on the hosted endpoint for small prompts, p95 jumped to 620ms under bursty traffic. We think batching might help.
[03:10] Ethan Blake: Thanks, that's useful. For the p95 jump were you using streaming or non-streaming?
[03:18] Owen Lee: Non-streaming for that run — easier for our downstream parser. We did a follow-up with streaming: p95 dropped to ~480ms but we saw increased CPU on our service.
[04:00] Ethan Blake: Right, streaming shifts some compute to client side for assembly. For SDK usage, did you try function/tool calls where the model returns a structured payload instead of free text?
[04:12] Owen Lee: Yep. We implemented a function call pattern: call the model, accept the JSON payload, then call our enrichment tool (internal API) based on the fields. Mostly good but sometimes the model's field names varied — e.g., "price_est" vs "priceEstimate" — so schema validation flagged that.
[04:45] Maya Patel: That name variance caused munged downstream records in one batch. We had to run a mapper step which adds latency.
[05:05] Ethan Blake: Two mitigations — a stricter output schema + Redwood's structured output enforcement (schema hints in the SDK) and a normalization layer on your side. We can also show how to use the SDK's structuredOutput option to enforce keys.
[05:26] Samira Khan: We'll share a concrete SDK sample that includes schema enforcement and example unit tests.
[06:00] Owen Lee: Awesome. One more note — KV cache behavior. During tests we saw some requests not benefiting from prefix caching. Not sure if it's a prompt/template mismatch or the way we call the tool.
[06:22] Ethan Blake: Could be prompt variability or tokenization differences. Also if you're doing function calls the cache may get invalidated when args differ. We can help reduce variability: canonicalize prompts and use the SDK's cache key hints. We'll share examples.
[07:10] Priya Rao: Security — we reviewed the SOC2 docs you shared. A few follow-ups: KMS integration for key rotation, SSO provisioning flow, and audit logs retention (7 vs 30 days). Also need clarification on data residency for logs during hosted benchmarks.
[07:40] Samira Khan: Good. We'll update the security pack. Ethan — can you attach the KMS integration guide and sample SAML flow?
[07:48] Ethan Blake: Yep I'll put both in the repo link. For logs we can limit what's sent during benchmarks and provide a redacted trace.
[08:25] Liam Torres: Back to structured output — our downstream is strict JSON, they'd like the model to always return an object matching schema, and an error field when uncertain. Is that supported?
[08:40] Ethan Blake: Yes — you can instruct the model via functions and structuredOutput config to return a JSON object with required keys and a confidence/error field. There is also Redwood-side validation to reject responses that don't conform. When that happens SDK returns a specific error code so your service can fallback to a safe path.
[09:15] Owen Lee: Perfect. Any recommended token limits? We saw a couple responses truncated mid-field when max_tokens was 256.
[09:26] Ethan Blake: For structured JSON, give a larger max_tokens buffer — 512 or 1024 depending on the expected payload size. Also prefer response_length hints in the prompt. If you need strictness consider using streaming + final validation before commit.
[10:05] Maya Patel: Cost question — when using structured output vs free text is there a difference in token billing?
[10:13] Samira Khan: Token billing is the same per token. But structured output tends to be more compact and predictable, so unit cost per useful field can be lower. We can show sample cost numbers from your test runs.
[11:00] Owen Lee: About tool calling — we tried a two-step where model suggests call A vs B, we then call internal enrichment, then call model again to aggregate. It works but latency multiplied. Any patterns to reduce round trips?
[11:20] Ethan Blake: Two approaches: 1) Hybrid prompts where model returns both the decision and a small candidate payload so you can batch enrichment calls in parallel; 2) Use Redwood's multi-tool orchestration — you can register tools and let the model call them (if allowed) which reduces hops because the runtime can optimize tool invocation and caching. However this goes into private deployment considerations for security.
[12:00] Priya Rao: Tool registration sounds sensitive — we need to control what tools can be called and audit them. Does Redwood provide RBAC on tool definitions?
[12:12] Ethan Blake: Yes RBAC for tool registration, audit logs for calls, and we have an allowlist model. For Private deployments you get an extra layer of network isolation.
[12:40] Liam Torres: On performance tuning — batching suggestions? We tried batch size 8, saw better throughput but tail latency rose. Any recommended autoscale/batch policies?
[12:55] Ethan Blake: Workload dependent — if you need lower p95, favor smaller batches and streaming. If you care throughput/cost, larger batches but accept higher p95. Redwood Optimize will suggest a sweet spot based on your request distribution; we can run that analysis on your traces.
[13:30] Samira Khan: We'll run Optimize on the traces you share and surface recommended batch sizes/quantization settings.
[14:00] Owen Lee: Regarding quantization — we experimented with an internal 4-bit setup on our infra but saw occasional subtle semantic drift on number extraction fields. Any guidance?
[14:13] Ethan Blake: Lower-bit quantization can change behavior for numeric extraction. For critical numeric fields keep a higher-precision variant or run A/B tests. Redwood has verified profiles per model that show accuracy tradeoffs; we'll point you to those.
[15:05] Maya Patel: Quick demo request — can Ethan show the SDK sample for function calling and structured output?
[15:15] Ethan Blake: Sure, sharing screen. (screen share) File open: example_app/integration/sample_function_call.js...
[17:30] Ethan Blake: Here's the key snippet: call model with functions: [{name: "extract_product", parameters: {type: "object", properties: {sku: {type: "string"}, priceEstimate: {type: "number"}}, required: ["sku"]}}], structuredOutput: true, max_tokens: 512. Then sdk.on('validationError', (err) => { // handle } ).
[18:10] Owen Lee: That validation hook is great — will wire it to a dead-letter queue for manual review.
[18:30] Priya Rao: On the security doc — one ask: can you confirm retention window for audit logs in hosted tier and if we can get longer retention for an enterprise package?
[18:45] Samira Khan: Yes hosted default is 30 days, enterprise adds longer retention options. We'll include pricing tiers in the SOW.
[19:10] Liam Torres: Any known limitations with VPC/private deployments for tool calling?
[19:22] Ethan Blake: In Private deployments you can register tools that are internal-only; network egress rules apply. There's more operational lift but you get full control. For POC we can simulate that with an allowlist and redacted traces.
[20:05] Owen Lee: One more practical: error handling pattern when model returns partial/malformed JSON — what's recommended? Retry? Ask for clarification?
[20:20] Ethan Blake: Recommended: validate, then if malformed either 1) call the model again with the prior context asking it to reformat, 2) use a deterministic parser/repair step, or 3) fall back to a safe path. We also provide a validation failure code so you can instrument metrics.
[22:00] Maya Patel: We ran your sample benchmark spreadsheet and saw cost estimates that are within expectations but want an extra run with our request distribution. Will share the sample set.
[22:20] Samira Khan: Great, please upload the sample set to the secure S3 link in the deck; Ethan we'll kick off Optimize there.
[23:05] Ethan Blake: I'll run Optimize and return recommendations for batch size, model variant, and quantization profile.
[24:00] Priya Rao: A compliance question — for keys: if we use our KMS (customer-managed) can Redwood rotate or does rotation have to be managed by us?
[24:18] Ethan Blake: We support customer-managed KMS with rotation controlled on your side; Redwood integrates and can do automated key use but rotation policy is yours. We'll document the flow.
[25:40] Owen Lee: Anything else on observability? We want token-level breakdowns and per-route latency.
[25:52] Samira Khan: Redwood Console gives token-level cost + latency per route. We'll provide demo access soon.
[27:10] Liam Torres: Let's recap next steps.
[27:20] Samira Khan: Recap: Samira will send pricing + SOW; Ethan will share SDK examples, repo link, KMS and SSO guides; QuantifyTech to run latency/correctness tests and upload trace; Redwood to run Optimize and schedule benchmark session.
[28:00] Maya Patel: Sounds good. Any blockers?
[28:05] Priya Rao: Security docs need clarifications but no block.
[28:20] Owen Lee: Engineering wants the example repo and a small checklist of integration tests.
[28:40] Samira Khan: We'll add a checklist to the repo.
[29:10] Ethan Blake: I'll include unit test examples for schema enforcement and a sample dead-letter queue pattern.
[30:00] Liam Torres: Cool. Anything else?
[30:10] (brief cross talk)
[32:00] Samira Khan: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the links and schedule the benchmark.
[32:10] Maya Patel: Thanks.
[32:12] Owen Lee: Thanks all.
[32:15] (meeting ends)
